dialogue.text: Steady, Wick. Hold it there. Don't fire through the wood.
Back up two steps. If it comes through, it comes through to me first.
Light on the hatch. Keep it there.
You're all right. Breathe. It's still on the other side.
(to the hatch) Still there? Good. So am I.

notes: Combat, round 1, your turn. Initiative: you 21, the drover-dogs 7. When your turn ends, theirs comes.
Your action this turn is spent: the stroke through the hatch missed. Your bonus action, your movement (30 ft), one object interaction and your reaction remain. Speech is free.

One of them lies against the outside of the hatch at your knee, on the other side of the planks. Your blade went through where you judged its head to be and met nothing. You heard a sharp hitch of breath, close. It has not moved off that you can hear. You cannot see it.

The indigo lightsaber is lit in your right hand, the blade run out through a slot it burned in the hatch planks low by the sill. The slot's edges are charred and smoking; no flame. The hatch is shut and bolted from inside, the bolt home. Your left hand is free; the rake is on the boards at your feet.

Wick is just behind you, his lantern up, your blaster lifted toward the hatch past your left side. You told him not to fire unless you are threatened. He has never fired a blaster. Your holster is empty.

Beyond the left wall: one lies still about 60 ft back up the floor, out in the grass; the other was last near the cart door. One lies against the outside of the small door, 120 ft up the floor, by your lamp. The small door is held only by a hook in an eye.
The voices outside repeat words they have heard, word for word, in the voice that said them: yours, and Wick's.
The voice down the rise calls every few minutes, the same words. It is due again any moment.
In your robe pockets: the folding knife (folded), the flat cell, three pairs of work gloves. In your backpack: the canteen, the dead datapad, eight rations. The comm at your collar is closed.
It is just over three hours since the sun went down. It will not be light for about twelve hours.

visible.label: Wick, standing just behind you, in PELL's coveralls and gloves; his open lantern up in his left hand; your blaster in his right, lifted off the boards, its muzzle on the hatch past your left side. He has not fired. His breath comes held and short.

Outside the hatch, at your knee: one of them, lying against the hatch boards at the sill, unseen. Your blade went through the planks at the place you judged its head to be and met nothing. A sharp hitch of breath on the other side, close; then nothing. It has not moved off that you can hear. Earlier, from out there, something said 'Mum?' in Wick's voice.

The far-end hatch at your knee, about 3 ft square, planked, at floor level in the far end wall: shut and bolted from inside, the bolt home. Your blade runs out through a slot it burned in the planks low by the sill; the slot's edges char and smoke. One of them lies against the outside of it.
The rake, lying along the walkway at your feet

The line of boot prints in the grain dust, running down the whole floor from the spill at her lantern to the sill of this hatch at your feet and stopping there, nothing coming back; an even walking stride; a small work boot, a woman's size, a ridged farm-boot sole. They run over sound boards all the way.

The board walkway running the length of the floor: you tested it end to end with the rake: every board knocks dead and solid, spiked down onto heavy sleepers on a hard floor; no space under it. Here in the dark half only Wick's lantern lights it; the strips' white light begins 60 ft back up the floor

Rows of low slatted drying beds either side of the walkway, grain spread level in them, undisturbed; each a slatted tray over a shallow closed air box, a hand deep, fed by a sheet-metal duct from the right-hand wall; nothing bigger than a rat could get in

Beyond the left wall: one of the two out there lies still in the grass about 60 ft back up the floor from you; the other was last near the cart door. Neither has made a sound since the call. Earlier, from out there, your own laugh and your own words: 'Wick, these dogs really are stupid. What was the name of the worthless leader? Sprinkles? Cupcake?'

The wide double cart door in the left wall, 80 ft back up the floor: two plank leaves on iron strap hinges, shut, an iron ring pull on each; the heavy squared timber bar across both leaves, home in both iron brackets. Barred from inside.

100 ft back up the walkway, in the white light: her hooded lantern with the blue tape on its handle, upright on the boards, out and cold, burned dry where it stands; beside it the bed raked level in even strokes to about halfway, rough past that, grain spilled onto the walkway.
The small door in the end wall, 120 ft up the floor, shut and latched from inside: the hook in its eye. Your lamp lies lit at its foot. One of them lies against the other side of it.
Outside the small door, 120 ft up the floor: one of them, lying against the door at its foot, unseen. You have heard nothing from it since it lay down.

Your lamp, lit, on its side on the boards at the foot of the small door, 120 ft up the floor; its light a small patch on the boards far off. Whatever lies outside that door is a foot from it, on the other side of the planks.
The switch box on the frame by the small door, 120 ft up the floor, its switch thrown; the strips lit over the near half of the floor
The fan housing and sheet-metal ducts along the right-hand wall, silent; branch ducts run in under each bed

feed.text: Sequence 1: Try: I quietly set the rake down; Try: I sneakily loose my saber hilt from the clip; Try: I look at Wick and signal to get ready, not making a sound; Try: I push the emitter of my lightsaber roughly where I think the dogs head is; Try: I push the button and ignite the saber through the hatch, ensuring I do not loose the bolt holding the hatch shut.

The far end of the drying floor is Wick's lantern and nothing else: thirty feet of yellow light on bare boards, the hatch at your feet, the end wall going up into the dark. The strips' white glow starts sixty feet back up the walkway. The small door, and your lamp lying lit at its foot, are a hundred and twenty feet behind you. On the other side of the hatch planks, close enough to touch if the wood were not there, one of them lies against the boards at the sill.

You lower the rake. The head finds the boards without a knock, the long handle follows, and it lies along the walkway at your feet. Your right hand goes to your left hip. The clip lets the hilt go with the smallest catch of metal, and the hilt comes up cold and unlit in your palm.

Behind you, Wick sees your signal in his own light. His jaw sets. He plants his feet in the oversized coveralls and lifts the blaster's muzzle off the boards until it points at the hatch past your left side, held out in his right hand, the lantern still high in his left. His finger stays where you told him to keep it. He makes no sound.

You bend low to the hatch, slow. The emitter touches wood low by the sill, a hand's width clear of the bolt, at the place where you heard it snuffle and settle. Through the boards, nothing changes.

You press the switch.

The blade goes through the hatch the way it goes through air. A snap-hiss, the hum climbing to its note, and the wood simply parts around the indigo light: a slot burned clean through the planks, its edges blackening at once, smoke curling up off the char in a thin grey thread. Indigo light spills out under the sill and through the cut, onto grass you cannot see. The blade runs on into the dark outside.

It meets nothing. No weight drags at the hilt, no hiss of burning hair, nothing but the steady thrum in your fist and the bitter smell of scorched wood filling the space under the end wall.

On the other side, inches from the boards, a sharp hitch of breath. Then nothing. No yelp, no scrabble of claws. The weight against the hatch is still there, and so is the silence it holds, listening.

The bolt sits home in its keeper. The hatch is shut. Behind you Wick's lantern shakes once and steadies, the blaster's muzzle on the hatch, his breath held. Somewhere out past the left wall the long grass is quiet. The call down the rise is due any moment, and it has not come.
